The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was established by municipal ordinance in 1977, with eligible police and fire employees hired from July 1, 1968, retroactively included. It has three closed retirement plans and a surplus benefit plan, designed to support recruitment and retention through retirement, disability, and death benefits. Plans I, II, and III closed to new members in 1977, 1984, and 1994, respectively, with varying 1994 closure dates for Plan III groups. nodes.title: A. Background Information
nodes.summary: APFRS was established by Anchorage ordinance in 1977, with eligible police and fire employees hired from July 1, 1968 retroactively included. It comprises three closed retirement plans, including a surplus benefit plan, providing retirement, disability and death benefits to encourage recruitment and retention. Plan I closed June 30, 1977; Plan II April 17, 1984; and Plan III closed on dates from May 24 to October 5, 1994, depending on employee group. A nine-member Board has exclusive fiduciary and administrative responsibility. The Director manages the system under Board direction and municipal code, supported by staff. Annual Board-commissioned actuarial valuations determine contributions, and independent audits are reported to the Board, municipal executives and Assembly. The investment consultant must provide objective advice, acknowledge fiduciary duties and be registered under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Proposers must review the sample contract; the successful bidder will enter a substantially similar contract. Services include annual investment-policy review, monitoring and alerts on managers and markets, watch-list oversight, and annual asset-allocation analysis considering objectives, actuarial assumptions, market conditions and efficient-frontier analysis.

nodes.title: Investment Consulting Work and Services
nodes.summary: The Investment Consultant provides objective, third-party fiduciary advice to help the Board make informed decisions about Retirement System assets and must be registered under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Proposers must review the sample contract; the selected proposer will enter a substantially similar agreement with the Board. Services include helping develop and periodically review an investment policy that reflects risk tolerance and supports return, funded-status, and administrative-expense objectives; reviewing the policy annually; monitoring and alerting the Board to significant manager-firm changes or market events; and designating and monitoring underperforming managers on a watch list.

nodes.title: 4. Investment Measurement Performance Reports & General Consulting Services
nodes.summary: The services include helping the Board review investment performance standards and guidelines; providing quarterly capital-markets, economic-conditions, and investment-market reviews and outlooks, plus annual long-term capital-market projections; and issuing monthly abbreviated performance reports within 20 days of month-end, covering monthly, quarterly, six-month, year-to-date, and 12-month results by manager, asset class, and total fund against benchmarks. Quarterly reports require 12 original copies within 45 days of quarter-end and manager and total-fund asset-allocation rankings across quarterly, year-to-date, trailing six- and 12-month, calendar-year, 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-year, and since-inception periods. Services also include assisting the actuary if needed; meeting the Board in Anchorage at least quarterly and presenting manager performance; attending and presenting at the annual investment review meeting, tentatively March 25–26, 2026; providing performance-attribution analysis; and reporting aggregate portfolio risk.

nodes.title: A. SERVICES OF CONSULTANT
nodes.summary: The agreement, dated on a blank date, is between an unnamed Consultant and the Board of Trustees of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System. It describes the Board’s responsibility for investing and administering the System’s assets, and the System as a public employee defined-benefit plan established under Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85. The Consultant will develop and review investment policies and guidelines; advise on asset allocation; and provide quarterly performance analysis, written reports, and Board presentations. Reports will review returns across investment types, show monthly and quarterly beginning and ending balances for each manager, analyze the Plan overall and by asset category, and discuss the investment environment, strategy, and recent performance. The Consultant will also monitor and report quarterly on managers’ compliance with System documents and policy, conduct manager searches when requested, and provide services in the April 15, 2025 request for proposal and other services agreed to and directed in writing by the Board and its Director.

nodes.title: B. RESPONSIBILITIES OF SYSTEM
nodes.summary:
B. RESPONSIBILITIES OF SYSTEM
The System agrees to provide or cause its accountants, trustees, investment managers and legal advisors to provide information regarding income, investment performance, and other pertinent matters relating to the System as requested by the Consultant from time to time. The System, through its Director, also agrees to communicate the System’s cash flow needs and investment goals to the Consultant and to keep the Consultant informed of changes in System’s financial or actuarial situation, needs and goals. The Consultant shall not be required to verify any information obtained from the System or its accountants, actuaries, trustees, and legal advisors and is expressly authorized to rely thereon. The Consultant shall verify all information obtained from investment managers.

nodes.title: C. CONFIDENTIALITY
nodes.summary: The Consultant must keep confidential all information about the System, Board, assets, investments, and financial transactions received while providing services, regardless of source or whether shared orally or in writing. During and after the agreement, the Consultant may use it only to perform services for the System and may not disclose it to third parties without the System’s written consent, except where disclosure is required by law. Confidential Information remains the System’s property. If a third party requests or demands disclosure, the Consultant must notify the System in writing within five business days and provide a copy of any written request or demand. The Consultant must take reasonable precautions to prevent unauthorized disclosure.

nodes.title: D. BASIS OF ADVICE
nodes.summary:
D. BASIS OF ADVICE
System acknowledges that the Consultant monitors and obtains information from a wide variety of publicly available sources and certain private sources. The advice provided by Consultant to the System is based on its analysis of such public and proprietary information.

nodes.title: E. REPRESENTATIONS OF CONSULTANT
nodes.summary: The consultant represents that it is unaffiliated with and uncompensated by the System’s investment managers; calculates returns using the GIPS time-weighted method; is professionally qualified and independent to evaluate investment managers; and is SEC-registered under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, with a duty to promptly report changes in registration. It must maintain at least $5 million in professional liability insurance throughout the agreement and provide proof before execution and annually during the first week of January. It also maintains a robust cybersecurity program to protect the System’s account information.

nodes.title: F. FEES TO CONSULTANT
nodes.summary:
F. FEES TO CONSULTANT
In consideration of the services rendered by Consultant, the System shall pay fees in accordance with Appendix A to this Agreement. Consultant shall not accept or receive, directly or indirectly, any commissions, fees, or any other form of remuneration or benefit of any kind, including, but not limited to, brokerage fees, “soft dollars”, “in-kind” services, or shared information, from any investment manager, custodian, broker, dealer, or any other person or entity in connection with or relating to the System’s assets, any investment made by the System, or any services performed under this Agreement.

nodes.title: G. MISCELLANEOUS
nodes.summary: The agreement covers only services specifically prepared for the System by Consultant or personnel designated in writing. Consultant acknowledges fiduciary duties under Alaska law and must prioritize the System’s interests. Neither party may transfer its rights or duties without the other’s written consent; the agreement supersedes prior understandings and may be amended only in a writing signed by both parties. The System acknowledges receipt of Consultant’s ADV Part II, to be updated annually. Alaska law governs; counterparts are valid, and the agreement takes effect upon execution. Claims must be brought in the specified state or federal courts in Anchorage, where venue lies; the prevailing party may recover costs and attorney fees. Consultant must notify the System in writing within seven business days of specified securities-related investigations or civil fraud, negligence, or fiduciary-duty actions. The parties’ relationship is principal and contractor, not employer and employee.

nodes.title: ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM
nodes.summary: The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS), established by municipal ordinance in 1977, provides retirement, disability, and death benefits to police and fire employees and beneficiaries. Its three plans are closed to new members, with closures occurring from 1977 to 1994. A nine-member Board of Trustees holds exclusive fiduciary and administrative responsibility; the Director and staff manage operations under Board direction and municipal code. Annual actuarial valuations determine contributions, while funding reflects employer and employee contributions and investment gains, less expenses and benefits. The Board commissions annual external audits, with valuation and audit results shared with municipal officials. The investment policy defines objectives and risk tolerance, performance standards, and guidelines for allocation, diversification, permitted investments, rebalancing, initiatives, oversight, and manager selection or termination. Investment goals are to fund current and future benefits, potentially increased when reserves exceed 116%, minimize contributions and costs, and target a 6.90% actuarial return. The Board also commits to prudent investing, diversification, and annual policy review informed by long-term projections.

nodes.title: II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
key_items: THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
nodes.summary:
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives
3to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals

nodes.title: III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
nodes.summary: The Board establishes long-term investment objectives for the total fund and each manager, considering the factors in the Investment Policy. The total fund should earn at least 5% above CPI-U, but no less than the actuary’s assumed return; outperform a custom index based on the target asset mix; and work toward 116% funding of each plan’s pension liability. Each year, 25% of identified surplus must be added to the contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. By simple-majority vote, the Board may distribute surplus under AMC 3.85. Surplus exceeding the additional reserve may fund enhanced benefits only with the actuary’s concurrence and recommendation, a Retirement Board supermajority, and an ordinance approved by the Anchorage Assembly. Manager agreements may set additional performance objectives and monitoring goals.

nodes.title: IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
nodes.summary: The section assigns investment governance duties: the Board sets policy and alone hires or releases managers, consultants, and the custodian; managers invest within policy and agreements; the custodian safeguards assets and administers securities lending; the Director implements policy, monitors providers, and deploys assets; and the consultant evaluates and reports performance, advises the Board, reviews policy annually, and assists with allocation changes. Assets must achieve the actuarially required return within acceptable risk. Trustees must act as prudent fiduciaries solely for members and beneficiaries. Allocation decisions consider tax-exempt purpose, liabilities, demographics, the closed system’s shortening horizon, liquidity needs, risk, and annual capital-market assumptions and asset-liability studies; allocations are reviewed quarterly and annually. The program specifies styles, benchmarks, and minimum/target/maximum ranges for equities, fixed income, real assets, and cash. Managers must have $500 million under management and a five-year performance record. Guidelines address diversification, security limits, credit quality, duration, derivatives, restricted investments, trading execution, commingled-fund deviations, and Board-approved exceptions.

nodes.title: III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
nodes.summary: The Board establishes investment policies for Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System assets, considering financial assumptions and investment risk, and has sole authority to hire, retain, or release managers, the investment consultant, and master custodian. Managers implement Board goals and policies, with discretion to select and diversify securities within policy limits and management agreements. The master custodian safeguards assets and administers securities lending agreements. The Director implements policies, monitors managers and custodian, and deploys assets within allocation parameters. The consultant evaluates manager performance, provides quarterly written reports and advice, presents results at regular meetings, annually reviews investment objectives, guidelines, and procedures, recommends amendments, and assists with interim asset-allocation changes when managers are added or removed. System assets must earn the actuarially required return within acceptable risk parameters. The text also introduces a Prudent Person Rule section without stating its provisions.

nodes.title: Investment Governance and Return Policy
nodes.summary: The Board alone hires, retains, and releases investment managers, the consultant, and master custodian. Managers carry out Board goals and may select and diversify securities within policy limits and management agreements. The custodian safeguards assets and administers securities lending. The Director implements policies, monitors managers and custodian, and deploys assets within allocation parameters. The consultant evaluates manager performance, provides quarterly written reports and advice, attends meetings and presents results, reviews objectives and procedures annually with recommendations, and assists with interim asset-allocation changes when managers are added or removed. APFRS assets are to earn the actuarially required return within acceptable risk parameters specified in V.C.4.

nodes.title: B. Prudent Person Rule
nodes.summary: B. Prudent Person RuleThe Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with similar aims.

nodes.title: C. Asset Allocation Factors
nodes.summary: The Board’s long-term asset allocation must account for the public system’s tax-exempt, fiduciary purpose; reliance on investment earnings, with possible member and municipal contributions; member demographics, liabilities, and the closed system’s shortening horizons, which call for increasingly conservative investments. Assets and managers must maintain enough liquidity for timely benefits, fees, and expenses, which may be deducted from portfolios. The Director and Investment Consultant review allocations quarterly and may reallocate overweight manager portfolios, reporting actions to the Board; illiquid alternatives may remain outside targets temporarily, and no action is required when allocations are within permitted limits. The Board reviews overall allocation annually and may reduce significant overweights, otherwise relying on consultant advice. Acceptable aggregate risk is defined in the policy’s Section V.D. Annual asset-allocation studies may establish long-term deployment rationale, set expected risk/return parameters, and reassess asset-liability alignment. Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and Consultant.

nodes.title: D. Asset Allocation Program
nodes.summary: The Board’s long-term asset allocation program defines investment styles, benchmarks, and minimum, target, and maximum allocations. It covers domestic large-, small-, and mid-cap equities; international equities; domestic fixed income; real assets, including real estate and farmland; and cash equivalents. Equity benchmarks include S&P 500, Russell, and MSCI ACWI ex-U.S. indexes; fixed income uses Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate, and real assets use NCREIF and other property/debt indexes. Major allocation ranges are domestic equities 22%/35%/48%, international equities 17%/23%/29%, total equities 39%/58%/77%, fixed income 19%/28%/40%, and real assets 4%/13%/23% (minimum/target/maximum). Cash has a target allocation and defined limits; the total fund target is 100%.

nodes.title: E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
nodes.summary:
E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
In order to be considered as a manager for the system a firm must meet the following minimum standards:
1. The firm must have at least $500 million under management;
2. The firm’s portfolio must have a 5-year investment performance history.

nodes.title: F. Manager Guidelines:
nodes.summary: Managers have discretionary investment-selection authority subject to law, trust documents, policy, and management agreements, and must follow guidelines on diversification, credit, duration, restricted transactions, and exceptions. Individual securities are capped at the greater of 5% or index weight plus 2%; purchases must trade on major exchanges or OTC. Listed ADRs are limited to 20%. Exchange-listed derivatives require advance disclosure of types, purposes, allocation, and risks; mortgage-backed securities must have a FLUX score of 15 or lower. Commercial paper must be P-1/A-1, and bond portfolios must average at least BBB+ under Bloomberg’s ratings methodology. Duration is capped at 120% of the Bloomberg US Aggregate Index. Prohibited activities include ERISA-related conflicts, jeopardizing tax-exempt status, letter stocks, borrowing, short sales, uneconomic tax-exempt bonds, private placements (except qualifying Rule 144A securities), and non-exchange-listed derivatives. Commingled-fund deviations must be reported for Board review; written exceptions require Board approval after consultant advice. Trades must seek best price and execution; the Board may use brokerage recapture or transition management based on consultant advice.

nodes.title: G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
nodes.summary:
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform (gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.

nodes.title: H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
nodes.summary: An Investment Consultant monitors the total fund and individual managers to maintain control of System assets without limiting managers’ initiative. The Board formally evaluates each manager quarterly, reviewing policy compliance, market opportunities, and risk-adjusted performance of managers and the total Fund. SIP performance expectations are considered reasonable over the long term. Review actions follow the Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure in Exhibit A, but the Board may terminate any manager whenever it determines, in exercising its fiduciary duty, that termination is in the best interests of the System and its participants.
